label: Chapter 3: The Gibraltar of the North, 1443 to 1815

units.text: If the first part of our story was about a dynasty, this part is about a rock.
For the next three and a half centuries, Luxembourg's main job in European politics was to be a fortress.
And it was a good one. A great deal of the time, the Luxembourgers themselves were not the ones deciding who owned it.
Philip the Good of Burgundy took the duchy in 1443, and for a while Luxembourg was one piece in a glittering Burgundian empire that included Flanders, Brabant and Holland.
Burgundy was the richest, most fashionable court in Europe.
But it did not last. In 1477, Philip's grandson Charles the Bold was killed in battle outside the city of Nancy, leaving a single daughter, Mary.
She married Maximilian of Habsburg, and through that marriage the Burgundian lands, Luxembourg included, passed to the Habsburg family.
This was the beginning of an era in which Luxembourg belonged to the most powerful dynasty in the world.

Maximilian and Mary's grandson was born in Ghent in the year 1500 and grew up to be Charles the Fifth, who ruled Spain, much of Italy, the Netherlands, Germany, and the new Spanish lands in the Americas.
Luxembourg was a tiny corner of his empire.
But it sat right on the road between his Netherlands and his Italian and Spanish possessions, so it mattered.
When Charles retired in the middle of the sixteenth century, his empire was divided.
His son Philip the Second took Spain and the Netherlands, and Luxembourg went with them.
That put Luxembourg in the front row for one of the great conflicts of the age.
The northern provinces of the Netherlands rose in revolt, turned Protestant, and eventually broke away to become the Dutch Republic.
But the southern provinces, including Luxembourg, stayed under Spain and stayed Catholic.
Luxembourg's people had barely been touched by the Reformation, and they remained loyal.
The seventeenth century was brutal.
During the Thirty Years' War, armies marched back and forth across the Luxembourg countryside, looting and burning.
Famine and plague followed the soldiers.
In some parts of the country, the population fell by something like half.
Meanwhile Spain was declining, and France under the Sun King, Louis the Fourteenth, was rising.
France began nibbling. In 1659, the peace treaty between Spain and France handed over a belt of towns along Luxembourg's southern border, including Thionville.
This was the first of several times that Luxembourg would shrink.
Then, in 1684, Louis the Fourteenth came for the fortress itself.
French forces besieged the city for about a month and took it.
And here the history of the place changes.
Louis brought the great military engineer Marquis de Vauban, the greatest builder of fortresses of his age, to rebuild the defenses.
Vauban dug ditches, raised massive walls, and tunneled deep into the rock.
Within a few years, the capital of Luxembourg was one of the most formidable fortresses in Europe, with a nickname that would stick: the Gibraltar of the North.
The French did not keep it. In 1697, after a long war, Louis gave Luxembourg back to Spain in the Treaty of Ryswick.

But France held it again briefly in the early eighteenth century, and when the great war over the Spanish throne was settled in 1713 and 1714, Luxembourg was handed to the Austrian branch of the Habsburgs, together with what is now Belgium.
Those lands became the Austrian Netherlands, and Luxembourg was a part of them.
The Austrian period, which ran for about eight decades, is sometimes remembered as a relatively calm and prosperous time.
Historians still debate whether it was really a golden age, but the evidence of peace is clear enough.
The population recovered. Ironworks along the rivers produced cast iron, and farming improved.
The Austrians kept strengthening the fortress, and in the 1730s they built a new fort on the plateau across the valley, called Fort Thüngen.
Its restored towers, nicknamed the Three Acorns, still stand today, and now they house a museum.
The real wonder of the fortress, however, was hidden.
Over the generations, engineers dug a vast network of tunnels, called casemates, into the sandstone cliff of the Bock.
They provided shelter for soldiers, space for cannon, and storage for supplies.
At the height of the fortress, there were many miles of tunnels.
Today, roughly seventeen kilometers of them survive, about ten and a half miles, and visitors can still walk through them and look out over the valley through the gun slits.
The fortress changed hands so often in this period that its history reads like a revolving door.
If you were an ambitious king, Luxembourg was a prize.
If you lived in Luxembourg, it was a burden.
The city was stuffed with soldiers, the townspeople paid for the upkeep of the walls, and every time a war broke out between France and its neighbors, armies tramped across your fields.
The quiet eventually ended in the 1780s.
Emperor Joseph the Second, who ruled from Vienna, was a reformer of the enlightened kind.
He tried to modernize his lands all at once, closing monasteries, limiting the church's power, and reorganizing the courts.
Many of his subjects in the Austrian Netherlands, including Luxembourg, were conservative and devout, and they were furious.
In 1789, the same year the French Revolution began, a revolt broke out in the Netherlands.
It was suppressed within a couple of years.
But the French Revolution was not so easily suppressed.
In 1794, French revolutionary armies swept through the Austrian Netherlands.
The Luxembourg fortress held out.
For about seven months, from the autumn of 1794, French troops surrounded it while Austrian defenders waited for relief that never came.
Finally, in June 1795, starving and cut off, the garrison surrendered.
Luxembourg, the Gibraltar of the North, had fallen, and not to a great assault but to hunger.
In the autumn of 1795, France formally annexed the territory.
The old duchy of Luxembourg ceased to exist, and in its place the French created a new administrative unit called the Department of the Forests, named for the heavily wooded Ardennes hills.
It was ruled from the city of Luxembourg.
The French years brought profound change.
The old feudal rights were abolished.
The church lost much of its land.
A new system of laws, the Napoleonic Code, was introduced, and traces of it survive in Luxembourg's legal system to this day.
But there was also a heavy price.
The French demanded soldiers. Young men from Luxembourg were drafted into Napoleon's armies, and many never came home.
In 1798, the conscription law sparked a revolt in the countryside of the north.
Peasants armed with clubs, farm tools, and old hunting guns rose up against the French.
The revolt is still remembered in Luxembourg by a name that means the Peasants' War, or more literally, the War of the Clubs.
It was crushed within weeks, and the leaders were punished harshly.
But the memory of it has never faded.
For generations, it was a powerful reminder of how deeply the ordinary people of Luxembourg resented foreign rule.
Then, in 1814, after Napoleon's disastrous retreat from Russia and his defeat at Leipzig, the French withdrew.
For the first time in centuries, the future of Luxembourg was up for negotiation among the great powers of Europe.
In the next chapter, they make a decision that creates something no one had ever seen before: a grand duchy.
